x: AP's sex ratio was 978 in 1981, 976 in 1991, 983 in 2001 and 997 in 2011. So it declined in 1981-91 (statement 1), then rose in 1991-2001 (976 to 983, statement 2) and again in 2001-11 (983 to 997, statement 3). All three statements are correct; '1 and 3 only' wrongly rejects the 1991-2001 rise.
key: Notes: AP sex ratio 978 (1981), 976 (1991), 983 (2001), 997 (2011) - declined till 1991, then improved, so statements 1, 2 and 3 are all correct

x: India's child sex ratio fell from 976 (1961) through 964 (1971), 962 (1981) and 945 (1991) to 927 (2001), and to about 918-919 in 2011 (provisional 914). So it was a decline from 976 to the 2011 figures; it never rose continuously or returned to 976.
The lowest child sex ratios in 2011 were Haryana (834) and Punjab (846). Option C swaps the two values; Mizoram (970) and Meghalaya (about 970) were among the highest, behind Arunachal Pradesh (972).

PLFS is a sample survey: it uses the same 7+ definition of literacy as the Census, but different samples, so its rates are not directly comparable with Census figures. The other options are false - neither uses a 15+ or 3+ definition, and neither excludes women or covers only urban or rural areas.

All three are correct: in the population-explosion phase (1951-1981) mortality fell rapidly while fertility stayed high, average annual growth was about 2.2%, and migration from Tibet, Bangladesh, Nepal and Pakistan added to the growth.

All three are correct: AP's median age is 32.5 against India's 28, its under-14 share is projected to fall from 25% (2011) to 15% (2036), and its 60+ share to rise from about 10% to 19% (2036) and 23% (2047).

Statement 1 is wrong: NFHS-6 was still unpublished in March 2026. Statement 2 is correct: AP's ST sex ratio was 1,009. Statement 3 is correct: India's NFHS-4 sex ratio was 991 (NFHS-5: 1,020). Hence '2 and 3 only'.
